strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: providing finite-sample statistical guarantees for LLM-as-judge pairwise evaluation, which is increasingly used to substitute for costly human annotation in benchmarking and RL pipelines.

BPE is a simple, cheap (only two forward passes), and intuitive mechanism to obtain a bias-neutral uncertainty signal by aggregating forward/reverse preference probabilities before computing entropy, directly targeting the well-documented position-bias failure mode of LLM judges.

The finite-sample FDR guarantee (Theorem 2.1) is rigorously stated and proved (Appendix A), and the linearized-loss calibration procedure is a sound way to avoid the instability of directly controlling a ratio of expectations on finite samples.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 3 benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena) x 4 judge scales (7B-70B) x 5 risk levels, averaged over 1000 random calibration/test splits, giving good statistical robustness to the reported risk/coverage numbers.

Reasonably thorough baseline comparisons for the uncertainty-estimation component (predictive probability, verbalized confidence, simulated annotators) and for the selective-judging component (vanilla, heuristic, naive calibration), with results showing consistent advantages for the proposed method.

Good reproducibility support: prompts, logit-extraction procedure, infrastructure, and hyperparameters are documented in the appendix; an honest limitations section acknowledges the exchangeability assumption, white-box requirement, and binary-judgment scope.
weaknesses: The core statistical machinery of SCOPE (linearized loss, finite-sample sufficient condition, largest-feasible-threshold rule, and the proof of Theorem 2.1) is a near-direct instantiation of the pre-existing LEC framework (Wang et al., 2025a) applied to the pairwise setting; the paper's stated 'twofold' contribution therefore leans heavily on this adaptation rather than new theory, which somewhat overstates the algorithmic novelty of SCOPE itself.

BPE is conceptually a fairly incremental combination of two long-known ideas — swapping response order to counter position bias (already used as a mitigation in Zheng et al., 2023) and predictive entropy as an uncertainty score — rather than a new insight into judge uncertainty; this limits the originality of the second contribution.

The claim that BPE 'mostly'/'consistently' outperforms baselines is not fully borne out by Table 1: verbalized confidence attains better ECE than BPE in several settings (e.g., Llama-70B on MT-Bench and RewardBench, Qwen-14B on RewardBench and Chatbot Arena), and the headline '2.4x more judgments' figure (Qwen-7B, MT-Bench) appears to be the most favorable single data point rather than representative of overall gains.

The most directly related prior work on selective LLM judging with guarantees (Jung et al., 2025, 'Trust or Escalate') is used only as a source for the simulated-annotators uncertainty baseline, not as a full selective-judging baseline in the SCOPE risk-control experiments (Table 3/Figure 2); omitting this comparison weakens the case that SCOPE improves over the closest existing guarantee-providing method for coverage/risk trade-offs.

Coverage at strict risk levels can be very low in practice (e.g., 0.018 coverage for Qwen-7B on MT-Bench at α=0.05), raising questions about the practical utility of the guarantee in exactly the settings (weaker judges, strict risk tolerance) where selective evaluation would be most needed.

The reliance on exchangeability between calibration and test data is a strong assumption that may be routinely violated in realistic deployment (e.g., evolving leaderboards, distribution shift across model generations, or adversarial/strategic responses), and while this is acknowledged in the limitations, no empirical stress-test of robustness to mild exchangeability violations is provided.

BPE requires white-box logit access, restricting applicability to open-weight judges only; since many practical LLM-judge deployments use closed API models (e.g., GPT-4-class judges), this substantially narrows the real-world applicability of the proposed uncertainty estimator, and no approximation for black-box settings is explored despite being flagged as future work.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: providing finite-sample statistical guarantees for selective LLM-as-judge pairwise evaluation, which is timely given the heavy reliance on LLM judges in benchmarking and RLHF pipelines.

Theorem 2.1 and its proof (Appendix A) are logically coherent and correctly adapt a linear-expectation-constraint style conformal risk-control argument to the pairwise FDR setting under exchangeability.
BPE is a simple, cheap (2 forward passes) and conceptually clean idea that explicitly targets position bias as a contaminant of uncertainty signals, rather than only accuracy.

Experiments span three benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena) and four judge scales (7B-70B), with extensive appendix detail on prompts, logit extraction, and infrastructure that aids reproducibility.
The comparison against naive/heuristic calibration baselines convincingly illustrates the practical value of a finite-sample correction term for avoiding risk-bound violations.
The limitations section is honest and identifies the exchangeability assumption, white-box requirement, and binary-only formulation as real constraints.
weaknesses: The core theoretical machinery (linearized loss, finite-sample sufficient condition, largest-feasible-threshold rule, and the overall proof strategy) is essentially a direct transplant of the concurrent/unpublished Wang et al. (2025a) 'LEC' framework into the pairwise-judging setting; the paper's own framing acknowledges this ('Following Wang et al. (2025a)...'), which limits the originality of the SCOPE component to an application rather than a new statistical methodology.

BPE's core mechanism (query both response orderings, average the resulting probabilities, derive an entropy score) is a fairly incremental combination of already well-known position-swap debiasing techniques (cited in related work, e.g., Zheng et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2025d) with a standard entropy-based uncertainty score; the technical novelty beyond this combination is thin.

The claim that 'BPE achieves superior calibration (ECE↓) ... in most settings' (Table 1 caption) is not well supported by the table itself: Verbalized Confidence has the best (bolded) ECE for Llama-3.1-70B across all three datasets and for several Qwen-14B/32B settings, despite having near-chance AUROC (~0.45-0.50), suggesting its apparently good ECE may be an artifact of near-constant/base-rate-matching confidence outputs rather than genuine calibration -- a confound the paper does not discuss.

Table 1 reports only point estimates despite the stated protocol of averaging over 1000 random splits; no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided, making it hard to assess whether the (sometimes small) AUROC/AUPRC gaps between BPE and baselines are statistically meaningful.

BPE requires access to model logits/probabilities, restricting applicability to open-weight models; the method as presented cannot be used with the closed, API-only judges (e.g., GPT-4-class models) that are arguably the most common choice in practice, which substantially limits the practical significance of the contribution (acknowledged only briefly in limitations without any black-box approximation or experiment).

Ties are excluded from all three benchmarks to fit the binary formulation, which likely removes a non-trivial and arguably more uncertainty-relevant subset of real pairwise comparisons, potentially inflating apparent calibration/discrimination quality relative to a more realistic deployment setting.

The abstract highlights a best-case statistic ('up to 2.4× more judgments... on MT-Bench with Qwen-7B'), which is a single favorable data point rather than a representative summary of the coverage gains shown in Table 3, several of which are more modest (e.g., RewardBench/Chatbot Arena coverage gains over Naïve are much smaller).

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem formulation that combines selective prediction/conformal risk control with a bias-aware uncertainty signal specifically tailored to the known failure mode (position bias) of pairwise LLM judges.

The finite-sample FDR guarantee (Theorem 2.1) is stated precisely and proved rigorously in the appendix via a linearized-loss/exchangeability argument, giving the method real distribution-free validity rather than heuristic calibration.

Thorough empirical evaluation: three benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena), four judge scales (7B-70B), five risk levels, and 1000 random calibration/test splits, which supports the stability claims (Figure 3) and gives reasonably convincing evidence that the empirical risk tracks the target α closely while coverage improves substantially over naive/heuristic baselines.

BPE is simple, cheap (two forward passes), and shown empirically to improve both calibration (ECE) and discrimination (AUROC/AUPRC) over predictive probability, verbalized confidence, and the more expensive simulated-annotators baseline (Table 1, Table 2).
Reproducibility is well supported: prompts, logit-extraction procedure, baseline configurations, and infrastructure are specified in detail in the appendix.
Honest and specific limitations section (exchangeability assumption, white-box requirement, binary-only setting, overhead) that does not overstate the contribution.
weaknesses: The core statistical machinery (linear expectation constraint calibration, Eq. 4-6, Theorem 2.1) is a direct adaptation of an existing method (Wang et al., 2025a) to the pairwise-judging setting; the theoretical contribution is largely an application rather than a new result, which limits originality on the SCOPE side.

BPE itself is a fairly simple combination of standard position-swap averaging (already common practice in LLM-judge literature, e.g., Zheng et al. 2023) with a binary-entropy transform; the novelty is incremental rather than conceptually new.

The method is restricted to binary pairwise judgments with ties explicitly excluded, which departs from realistic deployment settings where ties/near-ties are common and often the hardest cases to calibrate against.

BPE requires white-box access to logits, restricting applicability to open-weight judges; no empirical exploration of an API-only/black-box approximation (e.g., via verbalized or sampling-based surrogates) is provided despite this being flagged as important in the limitations.

The exchangeability assumption underlying the guarantee is strong and the paper does not empirically stress-test robustness to realistic violations (e.g., domain shift between calibration and deployment benchmarks, adversarial/strategic responses), despite motivating the problem partly via deployment reliability concerns.

Comparisons are limited to relatively simple internal baselines (vanilla, heuristic, naive calibration) and one external uncertainty baseline (simulated annotators); no comparison to other recently proposed conformal/selective LLM-judge frameworks cited in related work (e.g., COIN, SConU) is included, making it harder to assess relative significance of the coverage gains.

No analysis of how selective judging with SCOPE affects downstream uses explicitly motivated in the introduction (e.g., distorted model rankings/leaderboards or RL training signals), leaving the practical significance claim partly unsubstantiated beyond the risk/coverage metrics themselves.

strengths: Well-motivated and practically important problem: reliability of LLM-as-judge pairwise evaluation, with a clear articulation of failure modes (position bias, miscalibrated confidence, conservative statistical baselines sacrificing coverage).

The combination of a finite-sample conformal risk-control guarantee (SCOPE) with a bias-neutral, cheap (2-forward-pass) uncertainty score (BPE) is a sensible and practically useful instantiation for this application, and the paper provides a clean proof of the FDR guarantee (Theorem 2.1, Appendix A).

Extensive empirical validation: four judge model scales (7B–70B), five benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena, JudgeBench, PKU-SafeRLHF), 1000 random splits for statistical robustness, and a wide range of uncertainty baselines (predictive probability, verbalized confidence, swap-and-aggregate, simulated annotators, self-consistency) and selective-prediction baselines (vanilla, heuristic, naive, Trust-or-Escalate).

Thorough appendix ablations that meaningfully test robustness: label-noise injection on calibration data, calibration-set-size sensitivity, cross-benchmark transfer, and deployment on a specialized fine-tuned critic (Skywork-Critic) — these substantially strengthen confidence in practical applicability.

BPE consistently and clearly outperforms the closest baseline (Swap-and-Aggregate) on ECE/AUROC/AUPRC in essentially every cell, isolating the specific contribution of probability-level (vs. vote-level) aggregation.

Honest and detailed limitations discussion, including the exchangeability assumption, white-box requirement, and the extension to point-wise evaluation as future work; the cross-benchmark transfer ablation (Appendix H) further makes these limitations empirically visible rather than only stated abstractly.
weaknesses: Modest methodological novelty: the core SCOPE calibration procedure (linearized loss, finite-sample sufficient condition, largest-feasible-threshold selection) is explicitly adapted from very recent prior work (Wang et al., 2025b's linear expectation constraints and Angelopoulos et al., 2024's conformal risk control) rather than a new statistical technique; the main new ingredient is BPE, which itself is an incremental refinement of the existing Swap-and-Aggregate approach (replacing discrete vote agreement with probability-level entropy).

Practical utility at strict risk levels for weaker judges is quite limited (e.g., Qwen-7B on MT-Bench retains only ~1.8% coverage at α=0.05, and even ~24.6% at α=0.10), which somewhat undercuts the 'high coverage' framing in the abstract for realistic strict-risk deployment scenarios.

Cross-benchmark calibration transfer (Appendix H) shows clear violations of the nominal risk bound (up to 0.20 empirical FDR at target α=0.10) when calibration and test distributions differ in difficulty, which is a real practical concern for deployment since users may not always have in-distribution labeled calibration data matching the eventual test distribution; this caveat could be discussed more prominently in the main text rather than only in the appendix.

BPE requires white-box access to output logits/probabilities, restricting applicability to open-weight or API-exposed-logit judges; this excludes many popular closed judges (e.g., GPT-4-class models without logprob access for both tokens), somewhat limiting the generality of the 'drop-in' framing emphasized in the impact statement.

The main text's headline number ("up to 2.4× more judgments") and other efficiency claims are drawn from best-case comparisons in the tables rather than being consistently representative across all model/benchmark/α combinations, and the paper does not clearly quantify the average-case coverage gain, which would give a fairer overall picture.

Ties are excluded from all evaluated benchmarks to fit the binary Y={A,B} formulation, which simplifies away a common and arguably important real-world judging scenario; no discussion is given of how SCOPE would need to be adapted or how performance might change if ties were retained.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous finite-sample theorem (Theorem 2.1, with full proof in Appendix A) for selective pairwise LLM judging, and the empirical risk closely tracks the target α across five risk levels, four model scales, and three main benchmarks, which is a reasonably convincing demonstration of statistical validity.

The experimental protocol is extensive: 1,000 random calibration/test splits for statistical robustness, multiple uncertainty baselines (predictive probability, verbalized confidence, swap-and-aggregate, simulated annotators, self-consistency), multiple selective-prediction baselines (vanilla, heuristic, naive, Trust-or-Escalate), and several appendix studies (label-noise robustness, calibration-set-size ablation, cross-benchmark transfer, drop-in deployment on a specialized fine-tuned critic Skywork-Critic).

BPE is cheap (two deterministic forward passes) and empirically improves ECE/AUROC/AUPRC over the closest related baseline (Swap-and-Aggregate) in essentially every model/dataset cell, which is a clean, consistent, if incremental, empirical result.

The limitations section and several appendices (especially Appendix F and H) honestly report failure modes of the method, e.g., coverage collapsing under label noise and risk-bound violations under benchmark distribution shift, rather than hiding them — this transparency is commendable.
weaknesses: The core theoretical machinery (linearized loss, finite-sample sufficient condition, largest-feasible-threshold calibration) is explicitly stated to follow Wang et al. (2025b) 'linear expectation constraints,' which appears to be a very close concurrent/prior framework for selective prediction/routing; the paper's main theoretical contribution is essentially an application of this existing general risk-control machinery to the pairwise-judging setting, which limits the originality of the central claimed contribution (SCOPE) beyond domain adaptation.

BPE's novelty is incremental: it is explicitly described as sharing the same bidirectional prediction rule as Swap-and-Aggregate (Zheng et al., 2023) and differs only in replacing discrete vote agreement with averaged-probability binary entropy. While this yields consistent small gains, the 'bias-neutral' framing in the abstract/intro somewhat overstates the conceptual novelty of simply averaging two logit-derived probabilities, and no formal argument is given that averaging actually removes systematic position bias (as opposed to merely smoothing/reducing variance) when the two passes share correlated biases.

Appendix F shows that under realistic calibration label noise (15-20%, plausible for human preference data), SCOPE's coverage collapses to near zero in most configurations, raising serious doubts about the practical reliability of the framework when calibration labels are imperfect, which is the norm rather than the exception for human-annotated preference data.

Appendix H shows that calibrating on one benchmark and testing on another (even among closely related pairwise-judging benchmarks such as RewardBench vs. MT-Bench/Arena) can violate the target risk bound by up to 2x (e.g., risk 0.20 at α=0.10), directly undermining the practical applicability of the exchangeability assumption that the entire guarantee rests on, since in deployment the calibration and deployment distributions will rarely match exactly.

Reported coverage under the main results is often modest to low (e.g., 0.246–0.594 for weaker/mid-size judges on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena at α=0.10), meaning the method abstains on a majority of queries in many realistic settings, which weakens the core value proposition of using LLM judges to scale evaluation cheaply.

The method requires white-box access to softmax logits over the 'A'/'B' tokens, limiting applicability to closed, API-only judges, which are common in practice (acknowledged but not addressed with any approximation strategy).

Tie outcomes are excluded from all experiments to fit the binary formulation, which likely represents a non-trivial fraction of real pairwise comparisons and may reduce the practical/external validity of the reported coverage and risk numbers.

AUROC gains for BPE, while consistent, are often modest in absolute terms (e.g., 0.68-0.84 in many cells), suggesting the discrimination quality, while better than baselines, is still far from strong, which tempers claims about BPE enabling substantially more reliable selective judging.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem (reliability of LLM-as-judge in pairwise settings) with a principled finite-sample guarantee rather than a heuristic abstention rule, which is a meaningful step beyond prior conservative Clopper-Pearson/fixed-sequence-testing approaches.

The theoretical argument (Theorem 2.1) is stated clearly and proven in the appendix via a standard split-conformal exchangeability/linear-expectation-constraint argument; the authors are transparent that it follows the same identity structure as prior LEC work (Wang et al. 2025b), which aids reproducibility and correctness checking.

Extensive empirical validation across three main benchmarks (MT-Bench, RewardBench, Chatbot Arena) and four judge models, plus substantial appendix experiments: two additional benchmarks (JudgeBench, PKU-SafeRLHF), a specialized fine-tuned critic (Skywork-Critic), label-noise robustness, calibration-set-size ablation, and cross-benchmark transfer. This breadth strengthens confidence in the generality of the findings.

BPE is cheap (two deterministic forward passes) yet consistently improves ECE/AUROC/AUPRC over several baselines (predictive probability, verbalized confidence, swap-and-aggregate, simulated annotators, self-consistency) across nearly all model/dataset cells, supporting the claim that probability-level bidirectional aggregation yields a richer uncertainty signal than discrete-vote alternatives.

The limitations section is honest and specific (exchangeability assumption, white-box requirement, pairwise-only scope), and the cross-benchmark transfer experiment (Appendix H) candidly reports cases where the risk bound is violated under distribution shift, which is good scientific transparency rather than overselling the method.
The paper provides detailed implementation details (prompts, logit extraction, baseline configurations) that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: SCOPE's calibration procedure and validity proof are essentially a direct transplant of existing linear-expectation-constraint conformal risk control (Wang et al., 2025b) to the pairwise-judging setting, with the authors themselves noting the proof mirrors the single-model LEC derivation. The main original contribution is therefore BPE, which is itself an incremental refinement of the existing Swap-and-Aggregate idea (replacing a discrete vote with averaged probabilities and binary entropy).

The terminology "False Discovery Rate" is borrowed loosely from multiple-testing; the quantity actually controlled is a selective/conditional error rate (akin to selective risk in selective prediction), not an FDR in the classical multiple-comparisons sense. This could mislead readers unfamiliar with the distinction, despite the paper's definition being internally consistent.

Verbalized Confidence baseline performs at or near chance (AUROC ≈ 0.5) in essentially every configuration, including collapsing entirely on the specialized critic; this very weak baseline may be exaggerating BPE's apparent relative advantage, and the paper does not investigate why this baseline fails so uniformly or whether a stronger verbalized-confidence prompting strategy would narrow the gap.

Directly relevant recent selective-prediction-with-guarantees baselines for LLMs (e.g., the authors' own cited SConU/COIN works) are not included as baselines for SCOPE despite being closely related and plausibly adaptable to the pairwise setting; only heuristic thresholding, naive calibration, vanilla, and (in the appendix) Trust-or-Escalate are compared.

The evaluation excludes tie outcomes to fit the binary Y={A,B} formulation, which simplifies the task considerably relative to real-world deployment where ties/near-ties are common and often where judge unreliability is most acute; this restricts the practical scope of the reported guarantees.

The 1,000 repeated random splits are all drawn from the same fixed N=2,000 sample per benchmark rather than independent fresh draws from the underlying population, which may understate true variance across genuinely different data distributions.

Figure 2's 3D bar-chart presentation is difficult to parse precisely compared to a standard 2D line plot, and could be improved for clarity given the quantitative density of information being conveyed.
